newsitem.title: FRANCE: Corsica braces for formal end to guerrilla truce.
newsitem.headline: Corsica braces for formal end to guerrilla truce.

text.p: A small bomb exploded in Corsica on Friday as the troubled French Mediterranean island awaited the formal end of a separatist guerrilla "truce" already shattered by dozens of bomb attacks.

The 10-month-old truce declared by the hardline Corsican National Liberation Front (FLNC)-Historic Wing is due to expire on Saturday. But it has largely become a myth as attacks resumed after secret talks with Paris broke down during the summer.
The island's 1,700 policemen and paramilitary gendarmes, together with an undisclosed number of crack police squads, were on alert but kept a low profile, security officials said.
They said they feared attacks against conspicuous symbols of the French government, but were confident they could cope and had not called in reinforcements.

Police said a small bomb went off outside the post office in the town of Folelli, causing no injuries and little damage. It was the first blast since a bomb on Saturday night at city hall in Bordeaux, where Prime Minister Alain Juppe is mayor.
No one claimed responsibility for the Folelli bomb.

Some 20 post offices, often the only symbol of the central government in rural Corsica, have been bombed in recent weeks by separatists who have been seeking to loosen ties with the mainland in a two-decade old, low-key guerrilla campaign.
Police said last month they had arrested two young men who confessed to carrying out six such attacks recently. They are now in a Paris prison awaiting trial.

The FLNC-Historic Wing claimed responsibility for bombing Juppe's office in Bordeaux last weekend. The second Corsican attack on the mainland in a month, it led Paris to step up security in major French cities and announce a crackdown on separatists on the island.

Corsica's police chief Gerard Bougrier said police had for some time been stepping up searches for weapons -- a big task on an island whose 250,000 people have a tradition of owning weapons, if only for hunting in the densely wooded mountains.
There were conflicting calls for war and peace as the end of the "truce" approached.
The separatist group Fronte Ribellu (Rebel Front), an ally of the FLNC-Historic Wing, has called on the islanders to rise up against French "aggressors", branded "the hereditary enemy".
It threatened to kill anyone who helped police in the crackdown promised by Juppe against the separatists, who are split in rival groups waging a bloody war against each other.
More moderate nationalists called for dialogue and warned Paris that a brutal crackdown could revive support for the hardliners who have become increasingly isolated.
Gilbert Casanova, head of the Self-Determination Movement (MPA), called for an open dialogue with Paris and urged all islanders to rally in a "day for peace".
In Paris, the pro-government newspaper Le Figaro said the French people's patience was growing thin over the continuing trouble on an island heavily subsidised by the mainland.
"Each islander gets an average 27,000 francs ($5,400) in subsidies (annually). A record. But it's never enough...Violence and greed are the two bases of Corsican terrorism," it said.
It said the government must be firm but avoid falling into the trap of escalating violence that separatists hope for.
"Otherwise, France will some day...inflict the worst punishment on Corsica: grant it independence," it said.
